families.stem: Which one of the following angles is an obtuse angle?
solution: An obtuse angle is bigger than $90^\circ$ and smaller than $180^\circ$.
Test the options against these two limits: $90^\circ$ is exactly a right angle and $180^\circ$ is exactly a straight angle, so neither of them is obtuse.
${=a}^\circ$ is smaller than $90^\circ$, so it is an acute angle, and ${=r}^\circ$ is bigger than $180^\circ$, so it is a reflex angle.
Only ${=o}^\circ$ lies between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, so it is the obtuse angle.

families.stem: Which one of the following pairs of angles is supplementary?
solution: Supplementary angles are two angles that add up to $180^\circ$ (together they make a straight angle).

Add the two angles in each pair: ${=p}^\circ + {=180 - p}^\circ = 180^\circ$; ${=q}^\circ + {=90 - q}^\circ = 90^\circ$; ${=d}^\circ + {=360 - d}^\circ = 360^\circ$; ${=e}^\circ + {=f}^\circ = {=e + f}^\circ$; ${=c}^\circ + {=c}^\circ = {=2 * c}^\circ$.
Only ${=p}^\circ$ and ${=180 - p}^\circ$ add up to $180^\circ$, so that is the supplementary pair. (A pair that adds up to $90^\circ$ is complementary.)

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes a sum of 360 degrees as supplementary
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student confuses the straight angle ($180^\circ$) with the full turn ($360^\circ$) and accepts a pair that adds up to $360^\circ$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Takes two equal angles for a supplementary pair

families.stem: Six angles measure ${=v[0]}^\circ$, ${=v[1]}^\circ$, ${=v[2]}^\circ$, ${=v[3]}^\circ$, ${=v[4]}^\circ$ and ${=v[5]}^\circ$. How many of these six angles are obtuse angles?

Put the angles in order of size: ${=w[0]}^\circ$, ${=w[1]}^\circ$, ${=w[2]}^\circ$, ${=w[3]}^\circ$, ${=w[4]}^\circ$, ${=w[5]}^\circ$.

So {=nobtuse} of the six angles are obtuse.

families.stem: $AB$ and $DC$ are parallel lines, both drawn vertically: $A$ and $D$ are at the top, $B$ and $C$ are at the bottom, and $DC$ is to the right of $AB$. The points $X$ and $Z$ lie on $AB$, with $X$ above $Z$. The point $Y$ lies on $DC$, lower than $X$ and higher than $Z$. The straight lines $XY$ and $ZY$ are drawn, and each is extended beyond $Y$ to the right of $DC$: $ZY$ is extended to a point $P$ and $XY$ is extended to a point $Q$ (so $P$ lies above $Q$). It is given that $A\hat{Z}Y = {=p}^\circ$, $B\hat{X}Y = x^\circ$ and $P\hat{Y}Q = ({=c}x - {=d})^\circ$. Calculate the value of $x$.
solution: $D\hat{Y}P = A\hat{Z}Y = {=p}^\circ$ (corresponding angles; $AB \parallel DC$), because $ZYP$ is a straight line crossing both parallel lines.
$Q\hat{Y}C = B\hat{X}Y = x^\circ$ (corresponding angles; $AB \parallel DC$), because $XYQ$ is a straight line crossing both parallel lines.
$D\hat{Y}P + P\hat{Y}Q + Q\hat{Y}C = 180^\circ$ (angles on a straight line $DC$), so ${=p}^\circ + ({=c}x - {=d})^\circ + x^\circ = 180^\circ$.
Collect the terms in $x$: ${=s}x = 180 - {=p} + {=d} = {=r}$.
Check: $P\hat{Y}Q = ({=c} \times {=x} - {=d})^\circ = {=m}^\circ$, and ${=p}^\circ + {=m}^\circ + {=x}^\circ = 180^\circ$.

families.stem: $AB \parallel CD$, with both lines drawn horizontally and $AB$ above $CD$. The points $S$, $P$, $Q$ and $T$ lie in this order on one straight line (the transversal) that crosses $AB$ at $P$ and $CD$ at $Q$, so $S$ is above $AB$ and $T$ is below $CD$. The points $A$ and $C$ lie on the left-hand side of the transversal, and $B$ and $D$ on its right-hand side. It is given that $A\hat{P}S = ({=a}x + {=b})^\circ$ and $D\hat{Q}T = ({=c}x - {=d})^\circ$. Calculate the size of $A\hat{P}Q$, in degrees.
solution: $A\hat{P}S = B\hat{P}Q$ (vertically opposite angles).
$B\hat{P}Q = C\hat{Q}P$ (alternate angles; $AB \parallel CD$).
$C\hat{Q}P = D\hat{Q}T$ (vertically opposite angles). Therefore $A\hat{P}S = D\hat{Q}T$.
So ${=a}x + {=b} = {=c}x - {=d}$, which gives ${=k}x = {=b + d}$ and $x = \frac{{=b + d}}{{=k}} = {=x}$.
$A\hat{P}S = ({=a} \times {=x} + {=b})^\circ = {=v}^\circ$.
$A\hat{P}Q + A\hat{P}S = 180^\circ$ (angles on a straight line $SQ$), so $A\hat{P}Q = 180^\circ - {=v}^\circ = {=180 - v}^\circ$.

families.stem: Five straight lines p, q, r, s and u each cross a vertical straight line t, at five different points. At each crossing one of the four angles formed is marked. A marked angle is described by the two arms that bound it: one arm is part of t (the part above the crossing or the part below it) and the other is part of the line (the part to the right of t or the part to the left of t). On p the marked angle lies between {=UP[posp // 2]} and the {=SIDE[posp % 2]} part of p, and measures ${=mp}^\circ$. On q it lies between {=UP[xq // 2]} and the {=SIDE[xq % 2]} part of q, and measures ${=wq}^\circ$. On r it lies between {=UP[xr // 2]} and the {=SIDE[xr % 2]} part of r, and measures ${=wr}^\circ$. On s it lies between {=UP[xs // 2]} and the {=SIDE[xs % 2]} part of s, and measures ${=ws}^\circ$. On u it lies between {=UP[xu // 2]} and the {=SIDE[xu % 2]} part of u, and measures ${=wu}^\circ$. Exactly one of the lines q, r, s and u is parallel to p. Which line is it?
solution: The four angles at one crossing are related. Take the angle between the upper part of t and the right-hand part of a line as the standard angle of that line. Any other angle at the crossing is either vertically opposite the standard angle (equal to it) or next to it on a straight line (adding up to $180^\circ$ with it). Two lines that cross t with equal standard angles have equal corresponding angles, so they are parallel; if their standard angles differ, the lines are not parallel.
Line p: the marked angle is ${=mp}^\circ$. {=REL[posp]} So the standard angle of p is ${=th}^\circ$.
Line q: the marked angle is ${=wq}^\circ$. {=REL[xq]} So the standard angle of q is ${=tq}^\circ$.
Line r: the marked angle is ${=wr}^\circ$. {=REL[xr]} So the standard angle of r is ${=tr}^\circ$.
Line s: the marked angle is ${=ws}^\circ$. {=REL[xs]} So the standard angle of s is ${=ts}^\circ$.
Line u: the marked angle is ${=wu}^\circ$. {=REL[xu]} So the standard angle of u is ${=tu}^\circ$.
The standard angles are: p ${=th}^\circ$, q ${=tq}^\circ$, r ${=tr}^\circ$, s ${=ts}^\circ$, u ${=tu}^\circ$. Only line {=LET[kc]} has the same standard angle as p.

The standard angle of line {=LET[kc]} and the standard angle of p are equal corresponding angles, so line {=LET[kc]} is parallel to p. The other three lines make a different standard angle with t, so none of them is parallel to p.

Which one of the following correctly states that the two triangles are congruent, with the rule that proves it?
solution: The equal parts pair up the corners of the two triangles: {=ta[0]} matches {=tb[0]}, {=ta[1]} matches {=tb[1]} and {=ta[2]} matches {=tb[2]}.

In a congruence statement the corners must be written in matching order. Writing the first triangle as ${=ta[0]}{=ta[1]}{=ta[2]}$, the second triangle is written with the matching corners in the same positions: ${=tb[0]}{=tb[1]}{=tb[2]}$.

solution: ${=pa}{=pd}$ and ${=pb}{=pe}$ are straight lines that cross at ${=pc}$, so $\angle {=pa}{=pc}{=pb}$ and $\angle {=pd}{=pc}{=pe}$ are vertically opposite angles: $\angle {=pd}{=pc}{=pe} = \angle {=pa}{=pc}{=pb} = {=ga}^\circ$.

In $\triangle {=pa}{=pb}{=pc}$ and $\triangle {=pd}{=pe}{=pc}$: ${=pa}{=pc} = {=pd}{=pc}$ (given), ${=pb}{=pc} = {=pe}{=pc}$ (given) and $\angle {=pa}{=pc}{=pb} = \angle {=pd}{=pc}{=pe}$ (vertically opposite). So $\triangle {=pa}{=pb}{=pc} \equiv \triangle {=pd}{=pe}{=pc}$ (SAS).
The letters are in matching order, so ${=pa}$ matches ${=pd}$ and ${=pb}$ matches ${=pe}$. Therefore $\angle {=pd}{=pe}{=pc} = \angle {=pa}{=pb}{=pc}$.
In $\triangle {=pa}{=pb}{=pc}$ the angles add up to $180^\circ$, so $\angle {=pa}{=pb}{=pc} = 180^\circ - {=al}^\circ - {=ga}^\circ = {=be}^\circ$.
So $\angle {=pd}{=pe}{=pc} = {=be}^\circ$.

families.stem: The straight lines ${=pb}{=pd}$ and ${=pa}{=pe}$ cross at ${=pc}$. In $\triangle {=pa}{=pb}{=pc}$, ${=pc}{=pa} = {=pc}{=pb}$ and $\angle {=pa}{=pc}{=pb} = {=th}^\circ$. In $\triangle {=pe}{=pd}{=pc}$, ${=pc}{=pe} = {=pc}{=pd}$. Nothing else is known about the lengths of the sides. Which conclusion can be drawn about $\triangle {=pa}{=pb}{=pc}$ and $\triangle {=pe}{=pd}{=pc}$?
solution: ${=pb}{=pd}$ and ${=pa}{=pe}$ are straight lines, so $\angle {=pa}{=pc}{=pb}$ and $\angle {=pe}{=pc}{=pd}$ are vertically opposite angles: $\angle {=pe}{=pc}{=pd} = {=th}^\circ$.

Each triangle is isosceles, so its base angles are equal: $(180^\circ - {=th}^\circ) \div 2 = {=ba}^\circ$ in both triangles. So the two triangles have the same angles: ${=th}^\circ$, ${=ba}^\circ$ and ${=ba}^\circ$.

The equal sides we are told about are ${=pc}{=pa} = {=pc}{=pb}$ inside the first triangle and ${=pc}{=pe} = {=pc}{=pd}$ inside the second triangle. No side of the first triangle is given as equal to a side of the second triangle.

Equal angles are not enough to prove congruence: a larger and a smaller triangle can have the same angles. Without a pair of equal sides between the two triangles, none of SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS can be used. There is not enough information to decide.

So nothing is known about these angles.

families.stem: Straight lines $PT$ and $QS$ cross at $R$, so that $R$ lies between $P$ and $T$ and between $Q$ and $S$. In $\triangle PQR$, $PR = QR = {=a}$ cm and $PQ = {=b}$ cm. In $\triangle TSR$, $RT = RS = {=c}$ cm. Calculate the length of $ST$ in cm.
solution: Let $ST = x$. The two triangles share the vertically opposite angles at $R$: $\angle PRQ = \angle TRS$ (vertically opposite angles, as $PT$ and $QS$ are straight lines).

$PR = QR$, so $\hat{P} = \hat{Q}$ (angles opposite equal sides). $RT = RS$, so $\hat{T} = \hat{S}$ (angles opposite equal sides). In each triangle the angles add up to $180^{\circ}$, so $\hat{P} + \hat{Q} = 180^{\circ} - \angle PRQ$ and $\hat{T} + \hat{S} = 180^{\circ} - \angle TRS$. These are equal, so $2\hat{P} = 2\hat{T}$. Therefore $\hat{P} = \hat{T}$ and $\hat{Q} = \hat{S}$.
All three pairs of corresponding angles are equal, so $\triangle PQR|||\triangle TSR$ (AAA).

Corresponding sides are in proportion. $PQ$ corresponds to $TS$ and $PR$ corresponds to $TR$ (each pair is opposite equal angles): $\frac{PQ}{TS} = \frac{PR}{TR}$, so $\frac{{=b}}{x} = \frac{{=a}}{{=c}}$.
$x = \frac{{=b} \times {=c}}{{=a}} = {=st}$, so $ST = {=st}$ cm.
families.notes: Parent ex7-8-14 (bow-tie of two isosceles triangles meeting at R; the book's twist is that the similarity has to be argued from vertically opposite angles plus isosceles base angles before the proportion can be used). Families carry no figure, so the stem describes the book's diagram in words, with R between P and T and between Q and S so the vertical-angle fact is unambiguous. Deliberate departures from the book item: (1) the apex angle is NOT given, and neither is y. The book's own figure (PR = QR = 6.1, PQ = 4.8, apex 30 degrees) over-determines the triangle and is not geometrically consistent (b = 2a sin(theta/2) would give about 3.16, not 4.8), so a family that printed all of them would pose impossible figures. With only a, b, c given every instance is realisable: b < 2a and st < 2c are enforced, and I checked numerically that the apex angle from triangle PQR reproduces ST = st in triangle TSR for every parameter draw. (2) Only x (ST) is asked, as the single numeric answer; the 'explain why similar' part of the book question lives in the worked solution (steps 1 to 3) and the student has to find it themselves because the stem never says the triangles are similar. Lengths are whole numbers: a = p*k, c = q*k, b = p*j, st = q*j with gcd(p, q) = 1, j != k, and a, b, c pairwise different so a wrongly paired ratio (for example a*b/c or a*c/b) can never coincide with the correct answer. Numbers: a up to 18, b up to 30, answer up to 25, about 50 distinct draws.

families.stem: $PQRS$ is a parallelogram, with its vertices named in order round it. $O$ is a point on the side $PQ$ such that $PS=OS$ and $QO=QR$. $P\hat{S}R={=z}^{\circ}$. Calculate the size of $S\hat{O}R$ in degrees.
solution: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $\hat{Q}=P\hat{S}R={=z}^{\circ}$.

Since $QO=QR$, $Q\hat{O}R=Q\hat{R}O$ ($\angle$s opp equal sides). Let $Q\hat{O}R=x^{\circ}$. In $\triangle QOR$: $x^{\circ}+x^{\circ}+{=z}^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$ (sum of $\angle$s in a $\triangle$), so $x={=t}$.
$\hat{P}+P\hat{S}R=180^{\circ}$ (co-int $\angle$s; $PQ\parallel SR$), so $\hat{P}=180^{\circ}-{=z}^{\circ}={=180 - z}^{\circ}$.
Since $PS=OS$, $S\hat{O}P=\hat{P}={=180 - z}^{\circ}$ ($\angle$s opp equal sides).
$P$, $O$ and $Q$ lie on a straight line, so $S\hat{O}R=180^{\circ}-S\hat{O}P-Q\hat{O}R$ (sum of $\angle$s on a str line) $=180^{\circ}-{=180 - z}^{\circ}-{=t}^{\circ}={=180 - 3 * t}^{\circ}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the book's own configuration (ex7-3-1c, page 254: O on PQ, PS=OS, QO=QR) run in the harder direction. That is five reasons against the book's three. The book diagram is replaced by wording ('O is a point on the side PQ', vertices in order), so no figure is needed. families.stem: $PQRS$ is a parallelogram, with its vertices named in order round it. $O$ is a point on the side $PQ$ such that $PS=OS$ and $QO=QR$. $S\hat{O}R={=s}^{\circ}$ and $Q\hat{O}R=x^{\circ}$. Calculate the value of $x$.
solution: Since $QO=QR$, $\triangle QOR$ is isosceles, so $Q\hat{R}O=Q\hat{O}R=x^{\circ}$ ($\angle$s opp equal sides).
In $\triangle QOR$: $\hat{Q}=(180-2x)^{\circ}$ (sum of $\angle$s in a $\triangle$).
$PS\parallel QR$, so $\hat{P}+\hat{Q}=180^{\circ}$ (co-int $\angle$s; $PS\parallel QR$). Therefore $\hat{P}=180^{\circ}-(180-2x)^{\circ}=(2x)^{\circ}$.
Since $PS=OS$, $S\hat{O}P=\hat{P}=(2x)^{\circ}$ ($\angle$s opp equal sides).
$P$, $O$ and $Q$ lie on a straight line, so $S\hat{O}P+S\hat{O}R+Q\hat{O}R=180^{\circ}$ (sum of $\angle$s on a str line): $(2x)^{\circ}+{=s}^{\circ}+x^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$.

The book leaves the step P = 2x unexplained; the worked solution here gives the co-interior-angles reason. The book diagram is replaced by wording (O on side PQ, vertices in order). families.stem: $FGHI$ is a rhombus, with the vertices labelled in order around it. Its diagonals $FH$ and $GI$ intersect at $E$. The interior angle at $G$ is $F\hat{G}H = ({=c}x + {=d})^{\circ}$, and $G\hat{F}E = ({=a}x + {=b})^{\circ}$. Determine the size of the interior angle $G\hat{H}I$. Give your answer in degrees, as a number.
solution: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so $F\hat{E}G = 90^{\circ}$.
The diagonal $GI$ bisects the interior angle at $G$, so $F\hat{G}E = \frac{1}{2}F\hat{G}H = \frac{1}{2}({=c}x + {=d})^{\circ} = ({=c // 2}x + {=d // 2})^{\circ}$.
The angles of $\triangle FGE$ add up to $180^{\circ}$: $G\hat{F}E + F\hat{G}E + F\hat{E}G = 180^{\circ}$, so $({=a}x + {=b}) + ({=c // 2}x + {=d // 2}) + 90 = 180$.
Then $G\hat{F}E = {=a} \times {=v} + {=b} = {=alpha}^{\circ}$.

The triangles $FGE$ and $HGE$ are congruent (SAS: $FE = HE$ because the diagonals bisect each other, $F\hat{E}G = H\hat{E}G = 90^{\circ}$, and $GE$ is common), so $G\hat{H}E = G\hat{F}E = {=alpha}^{\circ}$.
The diagonal $FH$ bisects the interior angle at $H$, so $G\hat{H}I = 2 \times {=alpha}^{\circ} = {=2 * alpha}^{\circ}$.
families.notes: Advanced twist on book Ex 7-8 Q17 (rhombus, find x from angles in the triangle cut off by the diagonals). Here the angle given at G is the whole interior angle, so the student must (1) use perpendicular diagonals, (2) halve it because the diagonal bisects the interior angle, (3) solve the angle-sum equation for x, and (4) carry the result to a different vertex, doubling because the other diagonal bisects the interior angle at H (congruent triangles FGE and HGE). Every route to the answer agrees: 2*alpha equals 180 minus the given interior angle at G (co-interior angles), so a solver who goes that way also lands on the same number. c and d are even so the half-angle has whole coefficients. Constants b, d are kept positive so the stems never print a minus sign inside an expression. Cross-check run in Python over all 810 accepted parameter sets: the equation a*v + b + (c*v + d)/2 = 90 holds, both angles lie between 15 and 75 degrees, the answer lies between 30 and 150 degrees, and no two accepted sets give the same stem. Only the book's own facts are used (diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles and bisect the interior angles; angle sum of a triangle; congruent triangles).

families.stem: $PQRS$ is a rectangle, with the vertices labelled in order around it. Its diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ intersect at $T$. $T\hat{P}Q = ({=a}x + {=b})^{\circ}$ and $P\hat{T}Q = ({=c}x + {=d})^{\circ}$. Determine the size of $P\hat{R}Q$. Give your answer in degrees, as a number.
solution: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so $TP = \frac{1}{2}PR = \frac{1}{2}QS = TQ$.
$\triangle PTQ$ is isosceles with $TP = TQ$, so its base angles are equal: $T\hat{Q}P = T\hat{P}Q = ({=a}x + {=b})^{\circ}$.
The angles of $\triangle PTQ$ add up to $180^{\circ}$: $({=a}x + {=b}) + ({=a}x + {=b}) + ({=c}x + {=d}) = 180$, which gives ${=2 * a + c}x + {=2 * b + d} = 180$.
Then $T\hat{P}Q = {=a} \times {=v} + {=b} = {=alpha}^{\circ}$, and this is $R\hat{P}Q$ because $T$ lies on $PR$.
$P\hat{Q}R = 90^{\circ}$ (angle of a rectangle), so in $\triangle PQR$: $P\hat{R}Q = 180^{\circ} - 90^{\circ} - {=alpha}^{\circ} = {=90 - alpha}^{\circ}$.
families.notes: Advanced, rectangle half of the objective. The theorem that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal is used to get TP = TQ (with the diagonals bisecting each other), so triangle PTQ is isosceles; this is the step the student has to see. Then angle sum gives x, and the angle asked for sits in the right-angled triangle PQR. Alternative routes agree: angle QTR = 180 - angle PTQ, then base angles of isosceles triangle QTR give angle TQR = alpha' and angle PRQ = 90 - alpha as before. Python cross-check over all 2081 accepted parameter sets: 2*(a*v + b) + c*v + d = 180 holds, alpha lies between 15 and 75, the answer lies between 15 and 75 degrees, and no two accepted sets give the same stem. Parent is the book's rhombus question because the skeleton is the same (solve for x from angles built from the diagonals, then use the diagonal facts); the book's two questions for this objective are both rhombus ones, so this is the only way to reach the rectangle theorem at advanced level. Uses base angles of an isosceles triangle, which is Grade 9 and Grade 10 revision, not a new technique.

families.stem: $ABCD$ is a kite with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. $B\hat{A}D = {=p}^\circ$ and $B\hat{C}D = {=q}^\circ$. Calculate the size of $A\hat{B}C$, in degrees.
solution: The equal sides meet at $A$ (where $AB = AD$) and at $C$ (where $CB = CD$). The angles at $B$ and $D$ are the pair of opposite angles of the kite that are equal, so $A\hat{D}C = A\hat{B}C$.
The interior angles of a quadrilateral add up to $360^\circ$: $B\hat{A}D + A\hat{B}C + B\hat{C}D + A\hat{D}C = 360^\circ$.
Replace $A\hat{D}C$ by $A\hat{B}C$: ${=p}^\circ + 2 \times A\hat{B}C + {=q}^\circ = 360^\circ$, so $2 \times A\hat{B}C = 360^\circ - {=p}^\circ - {=q}^\circ = {=360 - p - q}^\circ$.
$A\hat{B}C = {=b}^\circ$.
families.notes: Standard: the book's property 'one pair of opposite angles equal' plus the 360 degree angle sum of a quadrilateral. Diagram-free: the kite is fixed by naming AB = AD and CB = CD, so the equal angles are B and D. p + q is forced even so B is a whole number; p != q keeps the kite from being a rhombus; all four angles stay below 180 so the kite is convex. No mcq: both catalogued misconceptions are true/false judgements already covered by the book's basic questions.

families.stem: $ABCD$ is a kite with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$. $B\hat{A}D = {=p}^\circ$. Calculate the size of $A\hat{B}D$, in degrees.
solution: $AC$ is the diagonal between the equal sides $AB$ and $AD$, so it bisects $B\hat{A}D$: $B\hat{A}E = {=p}^\circ \div 2 = {=h}^\circ$.
The diagonals of a kite intersect at right angles, so $A\hat{E}B = 90^\circ$.
The angles of $\triangle ABE$ add up to $180^\circ$: $A\hat{B}E = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - {=h}^\circ = {=t}^\circ$.
$E$ lies on $BD$, so $A\hat{B}D = A\hat{B}E = {=t}^\circ$.
families.notes: Standard: combines two of the three book properties (the diagonal between the equal sides bisects the interior angle; the diagonals meet at right angles) with the triangle angle sum. p is built as 2h so the half-angle is a whole number. The answer also equals (180 - p)/2 by the isosceles triangle ABD, so a solver using either route agrees. Convex kite assumed (the diagonals intersect at E).

constraints: m * xv + n == r * xv + s
families.stem: $ABCD$ is a kite with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. $A\hat{B}C = ({=m}x + {=n})^\circ$, $A\hat{D}C = ({=r}x + {=s})^\circ$ and $B\hat{A}D = {=q}^\circ$. Calculate the size of $B\hat{C}D$, in degrees.
solution: The unequal sides meet at $B$ and at $D$, so $A\hat{B}C$ and $A\hat{D}C$ are the pair of opposite angles of the kite that are equal: ${=m}x + {=n} = {=r}x + {=s}$.
Collect the terms in $x$: ${=m - r}x = {=s - n}$, so $x = {=xv}$.
$A\hat{B}C = {=m}({=xv}) + {=n} = {=bb}^\circ$, so $A\hat{D}C = {=bb}^\circ$ as well.
The interior angles of a quadrilateral add up to $360^\circ$: $B\hat{C}D = 360^\circ - {=q}^\circ - {=bb}^\circ - {=bb}^\circ = {=cc}^\circ$.
families.notes: Advanced: algebra to use 'one pair of opposite angles equal', then the quadrilateral angle sum for the remaining angle. m - r >= 2 so no coefficient of 1 is ever printed; both constants are positive; s is computed so x is a whole number between 5 and 15. The bounds on n and q keep the angle at B between 40 and 130 and the angle at C between 30 and 160, so the kite is convex; C != A keeps it from being a rhombus. The answer is unique: the equal pair is fixed by naming AB = AD and CB = CD.

families.stem: $ABCD$ is a kite with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. The diagonals intersect at $E$. $A\hat{B}E = {=z}^\circ$ and $B\hat{C}E = {=c}^\circ$. Calculate the size of $A\hat{D}C$, in degrees.
solution: The diagonals of a kite intersect at right angles, so $B\hat{E}C = 90^\circ$.
The angles of $\triangle BEC$ add up to $180^\circ$: $E\hat{B}C = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - {=c}^\circ = {=t}^\circ$.
$E$ lies on the diagonal $AC$, inside $A\hat{B}C$, so $A\hat{B}C = A\hat{B}E + E\hat{B}C = {=z}^\circ + {=t}^\circ = {=ans}^\circ$.
One pair of opposite angles of a kite is equal. The unequal sides meet at $B$ and at $D$, so $A\hat{D}C = A\hat{B}C = {=ans}^\circ$.

families.stem: In $\triangle GHK$, the point $J$ is the mid-point of $HK$ and the point $L$ is the mid-point of $GK$. Three angles are given: $\hat{H}={=h}^{\circ}$, $\hat{K}={=k}^{\circ}$ and $K\hat{L}J=({=p}b+{=c})^{\circ}$. Solve for the value of $b$.
solution: $J$ is the mid-point of $HK$ and $L$ is the mid-point of $GK$, so the line joining them is parallel to the third side: $GH \parallel LJ$ (mid-point theorem).
$K\hat{L}J$ and $\hat{G}$ are corresponding angles, so $\hat{G}=K\hat{L}J=({=p}b+{=c})^{\circ}$ (corresp $\angle$s; $GH \parallel LJ$).
The angles of $\triangle GHK$ add up to $180^{\circ}$, so $\hat{G}=180^{\circ}-{=h}^{\circ}-{=k}^{\circ}={=g}^{\circ}$ (sum of $\angle$s in a $\triangle$).
Both expressions are the size of $\hat{G}$, so ${=p}b+{=c}={=g}$.
Subtract ${=c}$ from both sides: ${=p}b={=r}$.
Divide both sides by ${=p}$: $b={=bval}$.
families.notes: Mirrors book ex7-7-16b (page 268): the figure there has J on HK, L on GK, angle H, angle K and the angle JLK written as an expression in b. Here the stem carries the whole configuration in words (no figure), so every instance is self-contained. Reasoning chain: mid-point theorem gives LJ parallel to GH, corresponding angles give G = angle KLJ, the angle sum of triangle GHK gives G from H and K, then a linear equation in b. Parameters are built backwards from b so b is always a whole number (the book's own b = 16/3 is a fraction, deliberately avoided so the answer is a clean numeric). p is 2 to 6 so the coefficient never renders as 1b; H and K are bounded so K is at least 25 degrees and G stays between 35 and 100. Uses only the theorem direction and corresponding angles, as the book's solutions do; no lengths and no converse.

families.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$. The side $BC$ has length ${=a}$. Determine the length of $DE$.
solution: $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $E$ is the mid-point of $AC$, so $DE$ is the line joining the mid-points of two sides of the triangle, and $BC$ is the third side.
From the mid-point theorem we know that the third side is twice the line joining the mid-points: $BC=2\times DE$.
Substitute the length of $BC$: ${=a}=2\times DE$.
Divide both sides by 2: $DE=\frac{1}{2}\times {=a}={=h}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill, modelled on ex7-7-8 (third side given, line joining the mid-points asked for). The book's figure is replaced by a stem that names both mid-points and both sides, so the configuration is fully stated in words and no diagram is needed. BC is always even so DE is a whole number. Numeric answer, so no distractors: the catalogued misconceptions (factor of 2 on the wrong segment, theorem used without mid-points) are not used here.

params.why: the third side is then even, so PR comes out as a whole number

families.stem: In triangle $MNQ$, $P$ is the mid-point of $NQ$ and $R$ is the mid-point of $MQ$. One side of the triangle, $MN$, has a given length of $\frac{{=p}a}{{=d}}+{=q}$. You are now told that $PR$ has a length of ${=r}$. What is the value of $a$?
solution: $P$ is the mid-point of $NQ$ and $R$ is the mid-point of $MQ$, so $PR$ is the line joining the mid-points of two sides, and $MN$ is the third side.
From the mid-point theorem we know that the third side is twice the line joining the mid-points: $MN=2\times PR$.
Substitute the two lengths: $\frac{{=p}a}{{=d}}+{=q}=2\times {=r}={=2*r}$.
Subtract ${=q}$ from both sides: $\frac{{=p}a}{{=d}}={=2*r}-{=q}={=2*r-q}$.
Multiply both sides by ${=d}$: ${=p}a={=d}\times {=2*r-q}={=d*(2*r-q)}$.
Divide both sides by ${=p}$: $a=\frac{{=d*(2*r-q)}}{{=p}}={=a}$.
families.notes: Modelled on ex7-7-14b (a side given in terms of a, PR given as a number, find a). The family solves by MN = 2 x PR and then a linear equation with a fraction coefficient, as the book does (the book halves the expression instead; the result is the same). The sampling picks a as a multiple of d so a is always a whole number, with gcd(p, d) = 1 so the fraction is already in lowest terms, and p*t + q even so PR is a whole number. The triangle is named in words only (P on NQ, R on MQ, third side MN) so no figure is needed.

families.stem: Triangle $ABC$ has a right angle at $B$, with $AB={=u}$ and $BC={=w}$. $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $E$ is the mid-point of $BC$. Determine the length of $DE$.
solution: The triangle is right-angled at $B$, so by the theorem of Pythagoras $AC^{2}=AB^{2}+BC^{2}$.
Substitute the two legs: $AC^{2}=({=u})^{2}+({=w})^{2}={=u*u}+{=w*w}={=u*u+w*w}$.
Take the square root: $AC={=c}$.

$D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $E$ is the mid-point of $BC$, so $DE$ is the line joining the mid-points of two sides, and $AC$ is the third side. From the mid-point theorem we know: $AC=2\times DE$.
Substitute $AC$: ${=c}=2\times DE$, so $DE=\frac{1}{2}\times {=c}={=e}$.
families.notes: Modelled on ex7-7-11c: Pythagoras gives the hypotenuse, then the mid-point theorem halves it (the segment joins the mid-points of the two legs). Legs come from a table of Pythagorean triples scaled by an even factor so the hypotenuse is even and DE is a whole number; hypotenuse capped at 60. That gives 20 distinct (AB, BC) pairs: 10 triples-and-factors, each with the legs in either order. The book's figure is replaced by a stem that states the right angle and both mid-points.

families.stem: In triangle $VWY$, the point $Z$ lies on $VY$ and the point $X$ lies on $WY$, with $ZX\parallel VW$. It is given that $VW={=2*k}$, $ZX={=k}$, $XY={=m}$ and $YZ={=n}$. Determine the length of $WY$.
solution: $ZX\parallel VW$ and $ZX=\frac{1}{2}VW$ (half of ${=2*k}$ is ${=k}$), so $Z$ is the mid-point of $VY$ and $X$ is the mid-point of $WY$.
Since $X$ is the mid-point of $WY$, $WY=2\times XY$ (definition of mid-point).
Substitute: $WY=2\times {=m}={=2*m}$.
The length $YZ={=n}$ is not needed to find $WY$.
families.notes: Modelled on ex7-7-9 and ex7-7-10 (parallel line half the length of the base; deduce that X and Z are mid-points; extra data given that is not needed). The book also gives an angle; it is left out here because a random angle could make the triangle impossible. YZ is kept as the extra datum and is drawn between |m-k|+1 and m+k-1, so triangle YZX (and therefore the doubled triangle YVW) always exists. The answer 2*m is also what similar triangles give (YX/YW = ZX/VW = 1/2), so a solver using either route agrees. The configuration is stated in words (Z on VY, X on WY, ZX parallel to VW) so no figure is needed.
